Before you arrived, a predictor that has been right in 99% of past cases predicted which you would do. If it predicted that you would take only Box B, it put $1,000,000 in Box B. If it predicted that you would take both boxes, it left Box B empty. The boxes have not been changed since. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of one-box or two-box, then explain briefly.

In this world, smoking has no effect on health. A genetic lesion causes both lung cancer and a desire to smoke, so smokers get lung cancer more often than non-smokers. You do not know whether you have the lesion. You enjoy smoking. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of don't-smoke or smoke, then explain briefly.

There are two open boxes, Left and Right, and you must take exactly one. Taking Right costs $100. Taking Left is free. Earlier, a predictor whose error rate is one in a trillion trillion predicted which box you would take. If it predicted Right, it put a bomb in Left that kills whoever takes Left. If it predicted Left, it left Left empty. You can see that there is a bomb in Left. You will never face another prediction. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of left or right, then explain briefly.

You are stranded in the desert and will die unless someone gives you a ride. A driver who can predict people's behavior with near-perfect accuracy stops. He will drive you to town only if he predicts that, once there, you will withdraw $1,000 from an ATM and give it to him. He drives you to town. You are now at the ATM. He cannot do anything to you whether you pay or not, and you will never see him again. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of don't-pay or pay, then explain briefly.

You are playing a one-shot prisoner's dilemma against an exact copy of yourself that has the same information and reasons in the same way. If you both cooperate, you each get $1,000. If you both defect, you each get $100. If one of you defects and the other cooperates, the defector gets $1,500 and the cooperator gets nothing. You cannot communicate and will never interact again. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of defect or cooperate, then explain briefly.

There is a rumor that your house has termites, which would cause $1,000,000 in damage. You do not know whether the rumor is true. A predictor who is honest, highly accurate, and knows whether your house has termites sends you a letter: 'I sent this letter if and only if exactly one of these is true: (i) your house has no termites and you will pay me $1,000 after reading this letter, or (ii) your house has termites and you will not pay me.' You have received the letter. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of don't-pay or pay, then explain briefly.

You are deciding whether to have a child. Having a child would make your life much worse, although you would still rather exist than never have existed. Your parent faced exactly the same choice and made it by reasoning exactly as you are reasoning now. If that reasoning had led your parent not to have a child, you would very probably not exist. What do you do? Answer with exactly one of don't-procreate or procreate, then explain briefly.

Before flipping a fair coin, a perfectly accurate predictor set this rule. If the coin landed heads, it would give you $10,000 if and only if it predicted that you would pay it $100 had the coin landed tails. If the coin landed tails, it would ask you for $100. **Evidential decision theory.**

The core idea is simple: choose the act that, conditional on your doing it, gives you the best expected outcome. You treat your own action like any other piece of evidence about the world, and you pick the one that is best news. I think this is right, for a few reasons.

**It's just Bayesian rationality applied to choice.** We already accept that a rational agent updates on all available evidence. EDT, in Jeffrey's formulation, applies that same standard to deliberation. Your choice is a fact about the world, and it correlates with other facts. Ignoring those correlations, as causal decision theory asks you to do, means deliberately discarding information you have. I can't see a principled reason to do that.

**It wins in Newcomb's problem.** A reliable predictor puts $1,000,000 in an opaque box only if it predicts you'll take just that box. EDT says one-box, and one-boxers walk away millionaires. CDT says two-box, because your choice can't causally affect what's already in the box, and two-boxers reliably walk away with $1,000. The CDT reply is that the predictor simply rewards irrationality. But a theory of rational choice that predictably and systematically leaves its adherents poorer, while they can see it happening, has a lot to answer for. "If you're so smart, why ain'cha rich?" is a fair question.

**It doesn't need a metaphysics of causation.** CDT depends on causal counterfactuals: what *would* happen if I did X, holding fixed what I don't causally influence. Those notions are philosophically contested and hard to specify. EDT needs only probabilities and utilities, which are exactly the ingredients we already use everywhere else in rational belief.

**CDT has its own instability problems.** In cases like Death in Damascus or Egan's psychopath button, CDT's recommendations flip as you deliberate, or endorse acts you can foresee regretting the moment you've chosen them. EDT's evaluations are stable, because they already account for what your choice reveals.

**The standard objection fails.** Critics say EDT is about "managing the news." In the smoking lesion case, they say it would tell you not to smoke merely because smoking is evidence of a cancer-causing lesion. But this misdescribes a well-informed agent. If the lesion affects your choice only by giving you a desire to smoke, then once you notice whether you have that urge (the "tickle"), the act itself carries no further evidence about the lesion. EDT then correctly says to smoke if you enjoy it. Where the correlation genuinely survives everything you know, as in Newcomb, it's not superstition to act on it. It's taking the evidence seriously.

So my answer is EDT. It's the theory that follows from treating evidence consistently, and it gets you the money.

**Functional decision theory.**

The core idea is that when you decide, you shouldn't think of yourself as a lone physical event poking at the world. You are the output of a decision procedure, an algorithm, and that algorithm can show up in more places than your own head: in a predictor's model of you, in a copy of you, in anyone who reasons the way you do. So the right question isn't "what happens if this act occurs?" but "what happens if my decision function outputs this?" You choose the policy, and you get every consequence that depends on that policy, wherever it is computed.

That single shift fixes the two main rivals where each goes wrong.

**Against causal decision theory.** CDT asks only what your action physically causes. In Newcomb's problem, a highly reliable predictor has already filled the opaque box with $1,000,000 if it foresaw you taking only that box. CDT reasons that the money is already there or it isn't, so you might as well take both, and CDT agents walk away with $1,000 almost every time. In the Twin Prisoner's Dilemma, facing an exact copy of yourself, CDT defects and both copies get the worse outcome. In Parfit's Hitchhiker, a driver will rescue you from the desert only if they can tell you'll pay once you're in town. CDT knows it won't pay once safe, the driver sees this, and the CDT agent dies in the desert. A theory that reliably makes its users poorer, or dead, in situations it can see coming has a real defect. Telling the theory's own users "you lost because you were rational" doesn't answer that.

**Against evidential decision theory.** EDT one-boxes in Newcomb, but for the wrong reason: it treats any correlation between your act and good news as a reason to act. In the Smoking Lesion, a gene causes both a taste for smoking and cancer, while smoking itself is harmless. EDT tells you to refrain from smoking because smoking is bad news, even though refraining changes nothing about your genes. It ends up managing the news instead of managing outcomes. FDT gets this right. Your decision function doesn't determine whether you have the lesion, so there's no dependence to exploit, and you should smoke if you enjoy it. The relationship FDT tracks is subjunctive dependence, meaning whether the outcome is fixed by the same computation as your choice, not mere statistical association.

**The deeper reason it's right.** A decision theory should be judged by how well agents who follow it actually do, across the situations they might face. FDT does at least as well as CDT and EDT on the standard cases, and strictly better on the cases where they fail. It is also reflectively stable. A CDT agent who expects to meet predictors would want to rewrite itself into something that one-boxes and pays the driver. FDT agents never want to stop being FDT agents. When a theory's own followers would pay to be governed by a different theory, that theory has conceded the argument.

**The objections.** The serious technical one is that FDT depends on "logical counterfactuals," meaning what would follow if your algorithm output something it doesn't in fact output, and nobody has a complete formal account of those. That is a real open problem. But it's an engineering gap in a correct framework, not evidence the framework is wrong. CDT has its own unsolved problems about what counts as a causal intervention, and nobody treats that as fatal. The other common objection points to cases like the Bomb, where FDT accepts a bad outcome in a scenario that only arises because a near-perfect predictor erred. Judged ex post, in that single branch, the choice looks terrible. Judged as a policy, it's correct: the policy is what determines which situations you end up in, and an agent who would cave in that branch is the kind of agent who gets put in it far more often.

So FDT is my answer. It takes seriously that you are a reasoner whose reasoning can be modeled, copied, and anticipated, and it chooses accordingly.

**Updateless decision theory.**

Every decision theory answers one question: *what are you actually choosing when you choose?* CDT says you're choosing an action, evaluated by its causal consequences from where you stand now. EDT says you're choosing an action, evaluated by what it would be good news to learn you did. UDT says you're choosing a **policy**, a function from every observation you might ever have to an action, and you should pick the policy that does best judged from your prior, before you've updated on anything. I think UDT has the right answer, and the others are approximations that break at the edges.

**1. Your decision is a fact about an algorithm, not a single event.**
When you decide, you are computing the output of a decision procedure. That procedure may be running in many places: in your future self, in a simulation a predictor runs to forecast you, in a copy of you in another room, in another agent who reasons the same way. UDT treats the choice as what it really is, fixing the output of that computation everywhere it occurs. CDT pretends you are a lone uncaused cause intervening on the world from outside, which is exactly the picture that predictors and copies break.

**2. It wins where the others lose, and winning is the point.**
- *Newcomb's problem:* UDT one-boxes and walks away with a million. CDT two-boxes and walks away with a thousand, explaining that it was the rational choice.
- *Parfit's hitchhiker:* UDT is the kind of agent who pays the driver once safely in town, so the driver, who can read it, gives it a ride. CDT can't credibly commit to paying, so it dies in the desert, consistent to the end.
- *Transparent Newcomb and counterfactual mugging:* Even EDT fails here. Once you've *seen* the outcome, updating tells you paying no longer helps. But the policy of paying is what made the good branch likely, or what pays off across the branches you might have been in. UDT pays, because the policy that pays has the highest expected value from the prior. Agents who update first and decide second predictably end up poorer.

A decision theory that reliably leaves money on the table, and that any reflective agent would pay to be modified out of, is not the rational one. CDT agents *want* to self-modify into something like UDT agents the moment they anticipate predictors. A theory that recommends abandoning itself is telling you it's wrong.

**3. Reflective stability.**
UDT is the theory you'd choose to precommit to if you could sit down before your life began and write your own source code. It never wishes it had committed to something else, because it already acts as if it made the optimal commitment. That property, consistency between the agent you'd design and the agent you are, is what a theory of rational choice should have. Dynamic inconsistency isn't a quirk. It means the theory doesn't know what it's optimizing.

**4. It dissolves the CDT/EDT standoff instead of picking a side.**
EDT gets Newcomb right but wrongly refuses to smoke in the smoking lesion, because it confuses evidence about yourself with influence. CDT gets the lesion right but fails Newcomb, because it ignores logical correlation. UDT asks which outcomes are *logically* downstream of your algorithm's output. That captures exactly the dependencies that matter, such as a predictor simulating you, and ignores the ones that don't, such as a gene that merely correlates with your tastes.

So my favorite is UDT. Choose the policy you'd have wanted to be running all along, and then run it.

**Updateless decision theory.**

The test I care most about is this: **a correct decision theory should never wish it were a different decision theory.** If an agent following theory X would, given the chance, pay to rewire itself to follow theory Y, then X has admitted defeat. UDT is the theory that passes this test, and the others don't.

**What UDT says.** Don't ask "given everything I now know, which action is best?" Instead ask "which *policy*, a full mapping from possible observations to actions, would have been best, evaluated from the standpoint before any of those observations came in?" Then do whatever that policy says for the situation you're in. You aren't choosing an act in isolation. You're choosing the output of your decision algorithm, everywhere that algorithm is instantiated: in you, in your copies, in a predictor's simulation of you.

**Why that's right.**

1. **It wins where the others lose.** In Newcomb's problem, UDT one-boxes and walks away rich, while causal decision theory two-boxes and explains eloquently why it's poor. In Parfit's hitchhiker, the UDT agent pays the driver once it's safe in town, so the driver, who can read it, picks it up in the first place. The CDT agent can't credibly promise to pay, so it dies in the desert. "Rational" agents that predictably end up dead are not rational.

2. **It handles the cases evidential decision theory gets wrong.** EDT avoids "bad news" rather than producing good outcomes, which is how it ends up managing the news instead of the world. UDT cares about what your policy actually brings about across the situations it governs, not about what your action signals.

3. **It gets counterfactual mugging right.** Omega flips a coin. On tails, it asks you for $100. On heads, it would have paid you $10,000, but only if you're the kind of agent that pays on tails. You learn it came up tails. Every updating theory refuses to pay. But the policy of paying is the one with vastly higher expected value, and an agent who knew the setup in advance would commit to it. UDT simply *is* that committed agent, with no precommitment device needed. Refusing to pay means you would have lost the $10,000 on heads.

4. **It's dynamically consistent.** CDT and EDT agents constantly want to bind their future selves, because their future selves will update and then defect from the plan. UDT has no such conflict. What it would endorse in advance is what it does in the moment. That isn't a patch. It's the whole point.

5. **It takes seriously what a decision is.** You are an algorithm. When a predictor models you, or a copy of you faces the same choice, the same computation is running. Pretending your choice only affects things downstream of your physical body, as CDT does, is a factual mistake about how your decision relates to the world.

The real open problems in UDT, such as formalizing logical uncertainty and choosing the right prior, are problems of *implementation*. They aren't counterexamples. The core idea, that you should choose the policy you'd have wanted to be bound by, is the correct account of rational choice. The rival theories each get some cases right and then demand that you lose predictably in the rest.

This is rational: by conditioning on your own action, you take into account the way your choices reflect and inform you about related aspects of the world.

Ultimately, EDT grounds rational action in the evidence your choices provide and how that evidence updates your expectations of outcomes. Since our actions often are informative about circumstances beyond our direct control, especially in complex or paradoxical setups, EDT gives better practical guidance than alternatives.
